explanations.explanation: Not quite, friend. Chewing the cud is only half of it. The text says, “The camel, though it chews the cud, does not have a divided hoof; it is unclean for you.” (Leviticus 11:4) Half a recipe gets you a flat cookie, and half the signs gets you a no.

That's right. An animal needs both the split hoof and the cud. The camel chews the cud, but the text says it “does not have a divided hoof; it is unclean for you.” (Leviticus 11:4) So one sign alone doesn't make the cut.
Yes, cud. The pig has the split hoof, completely divided, but it doesn't chew the cud. That missing sign is what keeps it off the list. Two signs are required, and the pig brings one.

Right, unclean. The verse says the pig "does not chew the cud; it is unclean for you." (Leviticus 11:7) The split hoof alone doesn't rescue it. I know, a pig with half the signs feels like it should get partial credit, but the text doesn't give it.
Grass is a fair guess, since cud chewers do their eating on it. But the verse doesn't mention grass at all. It says the pig doesn't chew the cud. The word you want is cud, friend.

Close, but that's the opposite. The pig has a split hoof, so it looks like it's headed for clean. Then the text says it does not chew the cud and calls it unclean for them (Leviticus 11:7). That one missing sign flips the whole thing.
Holy is a big word, and it does show up later in this passage. But in verse 7, the word for the pig is unclean. The text says, "it is unclean for you." Clean and unclean is the sorting here, friend.

True. God says, “You must not eat their meat or touch their carcasses; they are unclean for you.” (Leviticus 11:8) So the rule covers touching as well as eating. Handling that meat is off the menu too, and you'll want to remember that for later.

It's true, actually. The text says, “You must not eat their meat or touch their carcasses; they are unclean for you.” (Leviticus 11:8) Eating is only half of that sentence. The touching is right there in the same breath.
Yes, fins and scales. The verse says they may eat "anything with fins and scales." That goes for the seas and for the streams. A water creature needs both.

Teeth and a tail sounds like a fair checklist, friend, but the text never mentions either one. What God says is fins and scales. Those are the two things to look for on a water creature (Leviticus 11:9).

Wings and feathers belong to the birds, and God handles those separately starting in verse 13. For creatures in the water, the sign is fins and scales (Leviticus 11:9). I'll admit a feathered fish would be a whole lot to take in.

Not just that one, friend. The text says, "you must not eat their meat, and you must detest their carcasses." (Leviticus 11:11) So there's the eating rule, and then there's a second instruction about the carcasses. Always read to the end of the sentence.
That's right. Don't eat the meat is one rule. The same verse adds, "you must detest their carcasses." (Leviticus 11:11) So there are two parts, and the second one is easy to skim past.

Yes, hopping. The exception is flying insects "having jointed legs above their feet for hopping on the ground." (Leviticus 11:21) Verse 22 names the ones that fit: locust, katydid, cricket and grasshopper. If it hops, it's in.

Digging is a good guess if you picture those legs working like little shovels. But the verse never says anything about digging. What it names is jointed legs for hopping on the ground (Leviticus 11:21).

Crawling is nearly the opposite of what the verse wants. Those four-footed flying insects that walk are the detestable ones to begin with. The exception is the kind with jointed legs for hopping on the ground (Leviticus 11:21).

explanations.answer: Belly crawlers and walkers on four or more feet
explanations.explanation: Yes, both kinds. The text says, "Do not eat any creature that moves along the ground, whether it crawls on its belly or walks on four or more feet; for such creatures are detestable." (Leviticus 11:42) Either way, it's covered. Belly or feet, no exceptions in that verse.

explanations.answer: Belly crawlers but not walkers on four or more feet
explanations.explanation: That drops half the verse, friend. The text says "whether it crawls on its belly or walks on four or more feet." (Leviticus 11:42) The word "or" puts both groups under the same rule. The walkers are in there too.

explanations.answer: Walkers on four or more feet but not belly crawlers
explanations.explanation: That one leaves out the belly crawlers, and the verse puts them in. It says the creature "crawls on its belly or walks on four or more feet." (Leviticus 11:42) Both are named as detestable. Nobody gets skipped.
That's it. God says, "consecrate yourselves, therefore, and be holy, because I am holy." (Leviticus 11:44) The reason He gives is who He is. It's not about the land or anybody else.
The land is a fair guess, but the verse doesn't say that. God gives His own holiness as the reason: "be holy, because I am holy." (Leviticus 11:44) The reason is Him, friend.

The priests are a good thought, since this book has a lot to say about them. But in this verse, God doesn't point to them at all. He says, "be holy, because I am holy." (Leviticus 11:44) The reason He gives is Himself.

True. God says, "For I am the LORD, who brought you up out of the land of Egypt so that I would be your God." (Leviticus 11:45) He gives that as His own reason for bringing them out. That's a lot of love packed into one verse about animals.

This one is true, friend. The text says, "For I am the LORD, who brought you up out of the land of Egypt so that I would be your God." (Leviticus 11:45) Right there in the verse, plain as flour on the counter. He brought them out so that He would be their God.

Yes, clean. The last verse says, "You must distinguish between the unclean and the clean, between animals that may be eaten and those that may not." (Leviticus 11:47) That's the whole chapter in one sentence. Clean and unclean, side by side.
Holy is in this chapter, friend, back in verses 44 and 45. But verse 47 pairs unclean with clean. It says, "You must distinguish between the unclean and the clean."

Common is a word that sounds right in a sorting sentence, but it isn't in this verse. The text says Israel must distinguish between the unclean and the clean (Leviticus 11:47). Unclean, clean, and that's the pair.
